meta.what: 3 blind AI judges on every source the extension returned (production 618188c, before receipts)
meta.brief:
You are one of three independent judges building a gold-standard answer key. You will decide, for 155 pairs, whether a source BACKS a sentence from a student essay. Work alone. Do not look for other judges' output, other files in the goldset folder, or anything in the Tracely repo; use only the input file and the source pages themselves.

Input: judge-extension-input.json
Each item has: id, sentence, and the source's title, authors, publisher, venue, year, doi, url, and search_snippet.

IMPORTANT about search_snippet: it is what a web-search tool returned, and it may be paraphrased or invented. It is NOT evidence. Use it only to know where to look on the page; rely on a passage only if you see it on the page itself.

For each pair, choose exactly one label:
- "backs": the source states or directly evidences the proposition the sentence asserts, at the sentence's specificity. A source about the EFFECTS of X does not back a claim about how COMMON X is. A national figure does not back a local claim. For a sentence with two halves, the source must back the half that carries the checkable claim; if it only backs a minor half, use "topic".
- "topic": squarely on the sentence's topic and specificity, but it evidences a different proposition about that topic.
- "offtopic": a different topic, a broader or narrower level of topic, or a lexical collision (the right word in the wrong sense).
- "contradicts": the source states the opposite of what the sentence asserts.
- "unsure": you cannot tell from what is available.

Decide in this order and stop at the first answer: (1) Is it on this exact topic at this scale? If not, offtopic. (2) Does it address the specific proposition? If not, topic. (3) Then backs, or contradicts if it says the opposite.

Rules:
- Open the url (WebFetch) once per item to read the page, abstract or opening (if a doi is given and the url fails, you may try https://doi.org/<doi> once instead). Do not use your own background knowledge of the work; judge what the page shows.
- If the page cannot be read (fails, paywalled, empty), judge from the title alone. Use "backs" only if the title itself states the proposition; otherwise "topic", "offtopic" or "unsure".
- Be strict. "backs" means a student could cite this source for this sentence and a teacher who checked would agree.

Write your answers to:
judge-ext-LETTER.json

The format is a JSON object mapping each id to {"v": "<label>", "why": "<at most 20 words>", "read": true|false} where read says whether you could read the page. It must contain all 155 ids. Save progress to that file as you go (every ~20 items) so nothing is lost, and validate it with a quick script before finishing.

Report only: the counts per label, and how many pages you read successfully.
